newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, G7 outline plan for Chernobyl sarcophagus.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, G7 outline plan for Chernobyl sarcophagus.

text.p: Ukraine and its Western partners seeking the safe closure of Chernobyl nuclear power plant outlined plans Thursday to stabilize the crumbling sarcophagus built around the fourth reactor after it blew up 11 years ago.
Ukraine wants the sarcophagus, feared to be leaking radiation through cracks in its concrete walls, to be stabilized as part of moves to close the plant by 2000.
The two sides have held months of talks on how exactly to go about safely stabilizing the enclosure.

A multi-million dollar project running through to the year 2005 has been deemed cost-efficient and effective by the Group of Seven (G7) countries' representatives meeting on the problem, Carol Kessler, head of a G7 expert group, said.
"The project may cost as much as $780 million," Kessler told a news conference with Ukraine's Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko.
Ukrainian officials and G7 experts held talks in Slavutych this week, a small town which is home to about 5,000 workers who operate Chernobyl's sole working reactor.
The fourth reactor blew up on April 26, 1986, spewing radiation across much of Europe -- though 80 percent of the pollution hit neighboring Belarus.
The fate of the sarcophagus is the key to shutting Chernobyl, officials say.
"The first efforts will be to focus on ensuring the existing structure cannot collapse," Kessler said.

The project included stabilizing the structure's walls, building shields over fuel deposits still in the sarcophagus until they can be safely removed, and building some sort of shelter over it, she said.
Ukraine estimates 4,300 people have died because of the disaster, the world's worst nuclear accident.
